title: Elevator System
description: Design the control software for a bank of elevators in one building. Passengers call an elevator from a floor (up/down) and choose a destination inside the car. A controller decides which car serves each call, and each car moves, stops and opens its doors safely. Focus on how cars, requests, states and the dispatch policy fit together.

requirements.text: The building has N floors and M elevator cars; every car knows its current floor and direction.
Passengers press an up or down button on a floor (a hall call), and the system assigns a car to serve it.
Inside a car, passengers select one or more destination floors (car calls).
A car serves stops in its direction of travel before reversing, opens and closes its doors at each stop, and never moves with its doors open.
The dispatch algorithm (nearest car, least busy, zoning) must be swappable without changing the cars.
Each car has a weight capacity and refuses to move while overloaded.
A car can be put into maintenance or emergency mode, in which it stops accepting new requests.

constraints: Up to 50 floors and 8 cars in a single building.
All cars serve all floors unless they are in maintenance.
Time can be simulated in discrete ticks; no real hardware I/O.
Requests may arrive at any time, including while cars are moving.
Safety rules (doors closed while moving, no movement when overloaded) must hold in every state.
clarifyingQuestions: How many floors and cars are there, and do all cars serve every floor?
What should the dispatcher optimise for: passenger wait time, total travel time, or energy?
Is the direction (up/down) known when a hall call is made, or does the passenger only press 'call'?
Should a car serve requests strictly in arrival order, or sweep in one direction first (SCAN/LOOK)?
What happens to a car's pending requests when it is overloaded or goes into maintenance?

concepts.name: Elevator car
concepts.why: The car owns its current floor, direction, stops and capacity. It should move itself; a controller telling it every step turns the car into a data holder.

concepts.name: Car state (idle, moving, doors open, maintenance)
concepts.why: What a car may do depends on its state: it must not move with doors open or accept calls in maintenance. Making state explicit (an enum with guarded transitions, or the State pattern) keeps these safety rules in one place.

concepts.name: Dispatch / scheduling strategy
concepts.why: Choosing which car serves a call is the policy most likely to change (nearest car, least busy, zoning). It should be an interface the controller depends on, not logic inside the controller.

concepts.name: Central controller / elevator system
concepts.why: Something must receive hall calls and hand them to cars using the dispatch strategy. Keep it a coordinator: if it also moves cars and opens doors, it becomes a god class.

concepts.name: Request model (hall call vs car call)
concepts.why: Hall calls (floor and direction) and car calls (destination) carry different data and are routed differently: one goes to the dispatcher, the other straight to a car. Modelling requests explicitly makes queuing and ordering visible.

concepts.name: Buttons and panels
concepts.why: Buttons are where requests originate. Separating hall panels from in-car panels shows which requests go through dispatch and which go directly to a car.

concepts.name: Door
concepts.why: Door open/close and its safety interlock with movement is a responsibility of its own. Folding it into the car or controller hides the 'never move with doors open' rule.
